wine.name: Merengő Egri Bikavér Superior
wine.classification: Superior, the middle of the three tiers of Egri Bikavér
wine.grapes: Kékfrankos at the core, with Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Syrah in the vintage the house details; the mix moves with the year.
wine.sites: Several of the estate's vineyards in the Eger district, blended to a house style rather than for one site.
wine.making: Fermented for about three weeks in stainless steel or open vats, as the house describes it. The wine then ages for fifteen to seventeen months, by vintage, in 500 litre barrels of Hungarian oak, and rests in bottle before release, as the rules for the tier require.
wine.glass: Black cherry, ripe plum and blackcurrant with a peppery edge from Kékfrankos and a touch of cocoa from the barrel; deeper and firmer than a classic Bikavér, with ripe tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release after its time in barrel and bottle, it gains savoury depth over the next five to ten years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Eger's protected red blend of at least four varieties, with Kékfrankos at least 30 per cent of it.

records.table: Merengő is St. Andrea's Egri Bikavér Superior, a Kékfrankos led blend from the Egerszalók estate, aged fifteen to seventeen months in 500 litre Hungarian oak. Deeper and firmer than a classic Bikavér, it carries black cherry and pepper, and an hour of air opens it.
records.story: Bikavér means bull's blood, and the story goes that the name was born in the siege of Eger in 1552, when the castle's defenders drank red wine and the besieging Turks took it for blood. It is told as a legend: Hungary then made mostly white wine, and the earliest known document naming an Eger Bikavér dates from 1851. St. Andrea came much later. A family founded the estate in 2002 at Egerszalók, a village just outside Eger in the foothills of the Bükk, and named it in honour of the founder's wife; its wines of the late 1990s came before the estate. From the start the house built its range around Bikavér. By the house's account its first single vineyard Bikavér came from the Hangács vineyard at Demjén with the 2007 vintage, and Merengő took its place as the house's Superior, the blend made to a style across several sites rather than from one. In 2023 the district's rules were rewritten and Egri Bikavér gained a protected designation of its own. Merengő shows what the middle tier of the blend can be: Kékfrankos at the centre, more depth and grip than a classic Bikavér, yet fresh and peppery.

wine.name: Egri Bikavér Grand Superior Nagy-Eged dűlő
wine.classification: Grand Superior, the highest of the three tiers of Egri Bikavér, from one named vineyard
wine.grapes: Kékfrankos, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Syrah and Kadarka, planted together in the proportions of the intended blend.
wine.sites: The Nagy-Eged dűlő, a south facing block in the middle of the Nagy-Eged hill above Eger, pure limestone unlike the volcanic tuff of most of the district, its highest vines at about 500 metres; planted in 2008.
wine.making: The five varieties, planted together in 2008 in the proportions of the finished wine, are picked together and fermented together, rather than made apart and blended later. The wine then ages for eighteen months in wooden barrels and rests long in bottle before release, by the house's account.
wine.glass: Cassis, black cherry and red plum with violet and a peppery lift from Kékfrankos, cedar and a little cocoa from the barrel; firm, fine tannin and the bright, racy acidity of the limestone hill.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens some five years after the vintage and should hold its freshness for a decade and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; give a young bottle an hour or two in a decanter; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Five grapes planted together on the Nagy-Eged hill in 2008, then picked and fermented together: Thummerer's Egri Bikavér Grand Superior is a field blend from one slope, given eighteen months in barrel. Cherry, cassis and pepper ride on bright limestone acidity.
records.story: Vilmos Thummerer (1943 to 2021) and his wife leased their first vineyards from the local council in 1984, while Hungary was a communist state, and began making wine at Noszvaj, a village east of Eger in the Bükk foothills, where the family cellar is cut by hand into the volcanic tuff. In 1995 he was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year, and the house became a familiar name for Bikavér and Kékfrankos. In 2008 the family planted a block on the southern slopes of the Nagy-Eged, the limestone hill above Eger, with the five varieties of its intended blend in the proportions of the finished wine, so that the vineyard itself would make the cuvée: the grapes are picked together and fermented together. That wine became the house's Grand Superior, named for its dűlő. Vilmos Thummerer died in December 2021. The lesson of the Grand Superior is Bikavér as a field blend: one hill planted to a plan, rather than a cellar assembly of separate wines.

records.table: Leaner and firmer than its partner Síkhegy, Gál Tibor's Pajados Egri Bikavér Grand Superior is a single vineyard Bull's Blood of Kékfrankos and Kadarka with four other grapes. Wild fermented and aged in 500 litre Hungarian oak, it shows blackberry, plum and cinnamon.
records.story: Tibor Gál (1958 to 2005) was an Eger winemaker when, in 1989, after a visit and a tasting, he was invited to Tuscany by the founder of Tenuta dell'Ornellaia in Bolgheri. There he rose from cellar hand to chief winemaker, and the young estate made its name in his years. By the house's own account the family came home to Hungary at the end of 1992 and he founded the winery at Eger; other accounts date its start to 1993. One of his aims was to bring Egri Bikavér back to the standing it had lost, and he went on advising estates abroad as well. On 10 February 2005, returning from work at a winery in South Africa, he died in a road accident, aged 46. His son, who shares his name, took on the house and turned its Bikavér towards single vineyards: Síkhegy, on rhyolite tuff, and Pajados, the leaner and straighter of the two, both labelled Grand Superior, the uppermost tier of the blend. The winery carries the founder's name in the Hungarian order, family name first. In one bottle Pajados links Bolgheri and Eger and shows the straighter, firmer side of Bull's Blood.

wine.name: Egri Bikavér
wine.grapes: Kékfrankos at the core, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and other red grapes of the district such as Zweigelt and Blauburger; the mix moves with the year.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards in the Eger district, blended from several sites rather than one; the winery itself stands in an old stone quarry on the edge of the town.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel with the grapes' own yeasts, then aged in Hungarian oak barrels, a part of them new and small, for well over a year before blending and bottling.

records.table: Bolyki's Egri Bikavér is the everyday face of Eger's Bull's Blood: Kékfrankos led, aged over a year in Hungarian oak, made in a winery built into an old quarry outside the town. Black cherry, smoke and fresh acidity make it a red to open now.
records.story: Phylloxera reached Eger in 1886 and almost wiped out its vineyards, and the Bikavér blend of the twentieth century took shape in the replanting that followed, at the start of the twentieth century. Bolyki opens a newer chapter. It began in 1998, when a first generation winemaker, whose parents had grown grapes in their garden for a little extra income, planted the first vines on the Öreghegy at Verpelét. The house made its home in a disused stone quarry on the edge of Eger: walls some 30 metres high enclose the winery, and four pits joined by tunnels serve as its cellars. Around them the family built a range of Bikavér in each tier, a classic Egri Bikavér, a Superior and a Grand Superior from the Öreghegy, beside a varietal Kékfrankos that made the house known in the district. Since the rules of 2023, Egri Bikavér has held a protected designation of its own: a blend of at least four red grapes on a backbone of Kékfrankos. Bolyki's Egri Bikavér is the wine to teach the first step of the ladder: fresh, Kékfrankos led and released to drink, a Bull's Blood for the table rather than the cellar.

records.table: Gróf Buttler, Count Buttler in Hungarian, grows its Nagy-Eged Egri Bikavér Superior on the limestone hill above Eger, planted from 2003. Merlot and Cabernet led in the year the house details, it is round and firm, with fresh acidity under the fruit.
records.story: Eger's red wine story is younger than its white: by the district's own telling, red grapes such as Kadarka, and the way of fermenting on the skins, came with Serbs fleeing the Ottoman advance. After two years of preparation the Egri Bikavér regulations were adopted in 1997 and became official in 2002, the start of the tiers that a Superior label names. Gróf Buttler, Count Buttler in Hungarian, was founded at Eger in 1999, with its cellar in the old cellar row of Nagykőporos. It planted first on the volcanic soil of the Szarkás hill in 2000, and in 2003 it moved onto the Nagy-Eged, a limestone outcrop above the town whose vines reach about 500 metres, quite unlike the tuff of most of the district. In 2009 the house passed to new owners. By its own account it farms only its own vines and makes its reds the traditional way, in open vats and then in oak. Its Superior from the hill bears the hill's name. The rewrite of 2023 then gave Egri Bikavér a protected designation of its own. Set beside a Bikavér from tuff, this wine shows the limestone side of the blend, and how far its makeup could range from house to house.

others.note: Kadarka from the house's own vines, the old red grape of the Eger blend bottled alone.

others.name: Egri Pinot Noir Superior
others.note: Pinot Noir from the house's own vines, fermented in open vats and aged in oak barrels.

traps: Superior on this label is the middle tier, not the uppermost: Grand Superior, from one named vineyard, sits above it.
Gróf means count: Gróf Buttler is the name of a house founded in 1999, not the estate of a living noble family.

cards.front: Gróf Buttler: onto which hill did the house plant in 2003?
cards.back: The Nagy-Eged, a limestone outcrop above Eger, its highest vines at about 500 metres.

cards.front: Gróf Buttler: founded in which year, and where did it plant first?
cards.back: 1999; it planted first on the volcanic Szarkás hill in 2000.

questions.q: Which soil sets the vines of Gróf Buttler's Nagy-Eged Egri Bikavér Superior apart from most of the Eger district?
opts: The limestone of the Nagy-Eged hill
The rhyolite tuff of the Síkhegy
The black basalt of Somló
The deep loess of the Great Plain
questions.exp: The Nagy-Eged is a limestone outcrop, while most of Eger lies on volcanic tuff such as the rhyolite of the Síkhegy; Somló's basalt is a different district altogether.

questions.q: In which year were the Egri Bikavér regulations, which name the Superior tier on Gróf Buttler's label, adopted?
questions.exp: After two years of preparation the rules were adopted in 1997 and became official in 2002; 1851 is the earliest record of the name Bikavér at Eger, and 1886 the arrival of phylloxera.

report: Founded 1999 by the house's own page and a blog of 2012; Szarkás in 2000 and Nagy-Eged in 2003 rest on the house's page alone, as its own vineyards.

The count the house is named for could not be identified from two sources (a Count János Buttler of Mikszáth's novel A Strange Marriage is a candidate, his dates unconfirmed), so the story names no count.

The house's sheet for its 2018 Nagy-Eged Bikavér Superior lists no Kékfrankos at all (Merlot about half, Cabernet Sauvignon about a quarter, then Syrah, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Kadarka); the region record and the advanced quiz say Kékfrankos is compulsory, which holds for the rules of 2023 and may not have held for earlier vintages. The checker should weigh this.

A trade report says the house emerged from bankruptcy with a new team, which a former owner disputes; left out, and the pick may want a check that the house still makes this wine. Barrel length for this wine was not found, so the record gives the tier's minimum of a year, from Decanter and a second guide.

changed: story and the rules question: the 1993 draft standing as advice cut, found in no source; now adopted in 1997 after two years of preparation and official from 2002, as Magyar Bor gives it.
story: the change of owners in 2009 added as history, from The Drinks Business and Vinoport (no name); the farming of its own vines hedged as the house's account.
wine.sites, story and card: the hill no longer said to rise to about 500 metres; its highest vines reach about 500, the summit some 536.
wine.making: six months in bottle added to the tier's year in oak, as two guides give the Superior rule.
others: Nagy-Eged Kadarka now Egri Kadarka Superior, the label a merchant lists, its Nagy-Eged origin unconfirmed.
open: The house's sheet for 2018 lists no Kékfrankos while Decanter gives at least 30 per cent Kékfrankos for every Bikavér; the record states the house's blend for that vintage and does not say the rule held then.

A trade report of 2011 says the house was rescued from bankruptcy in 2009, which its former owner denied; the record says only that new owners came in 2009. The house's Nagy-Eged wine is a Grand Superior in some vintages (2015); a label with a vineyard name on a Superior is attested for 2018 by another house, so the pick stands.
